title: How Long Do We Keep It? Specimens and Records
summary: Sort specimens and records onto a timeline, see which retention periods come from CLIA law and which from CAP recommendations, and answer the add-on and inspector questions.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 1 Hits 5–6 and Number Vault rows 8–16 (retention). Separates CLIA legal minimums from CAP recommendations, which the reviewer presents together. The Number Vault concept (21 rows, incl. lab design and workforce figures) is not fully covered here, so it is not counted.

objectives: Give common retention periods for urine, serum/plasma/CSF, smears and surgical wet tissue.
Give retention periods for QC records, requisitions, blood bank QC, blood bank donor/patient records and cytogenetics reports.
Distinguish CLIA legal minimums from CAP recommendations and FDA blood-product rules.
Decide whether an add-on test request can be met, considering both retention and analyte stability.

scenes.title: Can we still test that tube?
scenes.altText: A doctor calls the lab two days after a blood draw asking to add a test to yesterday’s serum. The scientist looks at a storage rack and a calendar. A second request asks for a five-year-old blood bank quality-control record. Two question marks appear: how long must specimens and records be kept?

cues.text: Two days after a blood draw, a doctor phones: “Can you add one more test to that serum?”
The same week, an inspector asks to see blood bank quality-control records from five years ago.
Whether the lab can say yes depends on two kinds of retention rules: how long we keep specimens, and how long we keep records.

props.text: “Add one more test to Monday’s serum?”

scenes.title: Why things are kept — and for how long
scenes.altText: A timeline bar runs from hours to decades. Specimen chips drop onto the short end: urine 24 hours, serum, plasma, CSF and body fluids 48 hours, smears 7 days, surgical wet tissue 2 weeks after the final report. Record chips drop further along: quality-control records and requisitions 2 years, blood bank QC 5 years, blood bank donor and patient records 10 years, cytogenetics reports 20 years. A note says the farther a result’s consequences reach, the longer it is kept.

cues.text: Specimens are kept so the lab can re-test or add a test while the sample is still usable. Records are kept so anyone can later trace what was done, by whom, and with what quality control.
Specimens don’t last long. A common recommendation: urine for 24 hours; serum, plasma, CSF and other body fluids for 48 hours.
Blood and body-fluid smears for 7 days. Surgical wet tissue for 2 weeks after the final report.
Records last much longer. Quality-control records, requisitions and test reports: at least 2 years.
Blood bank quality-control records: 5 years. Blood bank donor and patient records: 10 years. Cytogenetics reports: 20 years.
The pattern: the longer a result can still matter to a patient or their family, the longer the lab keeps it.

scenes.title: Law minimum vs recommendation
scenes.altText: Two stacked layers: the bottom layer, labelled CLIA (federal law), shows minimums such as 2 years for most records, 5 years for cytology slides, 10 years for pathology reports and histopathology slides, and 2 years for paraffin blocks. The top layer, CAP recommendations, raises some of them — for example, paraffin blocks to 10 years. A third layer for state law and the laboratory director sits on top. A blood-product record chip is labelled 10 years by FDA rule.

cues.text: Where do these numbers come from? The bottom layer is the law. Under CLIA, most lab records — requisitions, QC and patient test records, proficiency testing, reports — must be kept at least 2 years.
CLIA sets longer floors for some items: cytology slides 5 years, pathology reports and histopathology slides 10 years, and pathology blocks 2 years.
On top of the law, accreditors such as CAP recommend periods that meet or exceed CLIA. For example, CAP recommends keeping surgical paraffin blocks 10 years, not 2.
Blood bank records follow FDA rules too: individual blood-product records are kept at least 10 years.
And state laws or the laboratory director can require longer still. So the exam question is usually: which is the minimum, and who sets it?

scenes.title: At the bench: answering the two calls
scenes.altText: Back to the opening calls. The 2-day-old serum is still within the 48-hour window only if it was drawn less than 48 hours ago and stored properly — and the new test must be valid on stored serum. The blood bank QC record from five years ago is still within the 5-year retention period. A checklist reminds that stability of the analyte, not just the retention rule, decides whether an add-on is valid.

cues.text: Back to the phone call. Serum is typically kept 48 hours. A sample drawn just under two days ago may still be on the rack.
But being on the rack isn’t enough. The analyte must be stable in stored serum for that long, or the add-on result can’t be trusted.
Now the inspector. Blood bank QC records are kept 5 years, so a five-year-old record should still be available — just.
Most labs keep a written retention policy that lists every specimen and record type, based on the strictest rule that applies to them.
If a lab closes, it must still arrange for its records, slides and blocks to stay available for the required time.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: A short staircase of specimen times and a tall ladder of record times sit side by side, with the CLIA floor beneath both.

cues.text: Labs keep specimens for hours to weeks so they can re-test, and records for years — at least the CLIA minimum, often longer by CAP, FDA, state or director rules — so that results can always be traced.

props.label: Floor: CLIA minimum · above it: CAP, FDA, state, director

explanation.what: Plain language: a lab keeps two kinds of things after testing — the leftover specimens, for a short time, and the paperwork (records), for years. Scientific terms: specimen retention and record retention. Common minimums: urine 24 hours; serum, plasma, CSF and body fluids 48 hours; blood and body-fluid smears 7 days; surgical wet tissue 2 weeks after the final report; QC records, requisitions, patient test records and reports at least 2 years; blood bank QC 5 years; blood bank donor and patient records 10 years; cytogenetics reports 20 years.
explanation.why: Specimens are kept so a test can be repeated or added while the sample is still usable; most analytes do not stay stable for long, so retention is short. Records are kept so that anyone — an inspector, a clinician, an investigator after a transfusion reaction — can trace what was done, when, by whom and under what quality control. The longer a result can matter (a transfusion history, a cancer diagnosis, a heritable chromosome finding), the longer the record is kept.
explanation.measure: This is an operations concept: the lab follows a written retention policy that lists every specimen and record type and uses the strictest rule that applies. When an add-on request arrives, the lab checks both that the specimen is still within its retention period and that the requested analyte is stable in that stored specimen. If a lab ceases operation, it must still arrange for its records, slides, blocks and tissue to remain available for the required time.
explanation.differs: CLIA (42 CFR 493.1105) sets federal minimums: most records 2 years, cytology slides 5 years, pathology reports and histopathology slides 10 years, pathology blocks 2 years, and tissue until diagnosis. CAP recommends periods that meet or exceed CLIA — for example, surgical paraffin blocks 10 years and cytogenetics reports 20 years. FDA rules (21 CFR 606.160) require individual blood-product records for at least 10 years. State law or the laboratory director may require longer.
explanation.examAngle: Expect direct recall (how long are QC records kept? how long is urine kept?), the 2-5-10-20 record sequence, and questions that test whether you know a value is a legal minimum (CLIA) or an accreditor recommendation (CAP). Pathology blocks (CLIA 2 years vs CAP 10 years) are a common way to test that distinction.

mnemonic.text: Specimens climb a short staircase (24 h → 48 h → 7 d → 2 wk); records climb a tall ladder (2 → 5 → 10 → 20 years).
mnemonic.explanation: The staircase is urine, serum/plasma/CSF, smears and wet tissue; the ladder is QC and requisitions, blood bank QC, blood bank donor and patient records, and cytogenetics reports. Higher stakes, higher rung.
mnemonic.limitation: These are common minimums blending CLIA and CAP. Some items sit elsewhere (pathology reports and histopathology slides are 10 years; cytology slides 5; CLIA keeps blocks 2 years while CAP recommends 10), and state law or the laboratory director can extend any period. The staircase also says nothing about analyte stability, which decides whether an add-on is valid.

analogyLimitations: The timeline is not to scale: hours and decades are squeezed onto one bar.
Chips and documents stand for categories; real retention policies list many more item types (e.g. instrument maintenance, flow cytometry plots, autopsy material).
Numbers shown are the minimums named in the cited sources; local policy may be longer.
takeaway: Labs keep specimens for hours to weeks so they can re-test, and records for years — at least the CLIA minimum, often longer by CAP, FDA, state or director rules — so that results can always be traced.

questions.stem: Under CLIA, what is the minimum retention period for quality control records and test requisitions?

options.rationale: Correct. CLIA (42 CFR 493.1105) requires test requisitions, QC and patient test records, proficiency testing records and test reports to be kept for at least 2 years.
Incorrect. Five years is the period for cytology slides (CLIA) and for blood bank QC records (CAP recommendation), not general QC records.
Incorrect. Ten years applies to pathology reports and histopathology slides (CLIA) and to blood bank donor/patient records — not general QC records.
Incorrect. Twenty years is CAP’s recommendation for cytogenetics reports and images.

questions.stem: A physician asks to add a test to a urine specimen collected 30 hours ago. The lab follows the common CAP recommendations. What is the most likely answer?

options.text: The specimen has probably been discarded; urine is commonly kept for 24 hours, so a new specimen is needed
options.rationale: Correct. CAP recommends keeping urine 24 hours (exceptions at the laboratory director’s discretion). At 30 hours the specimen is likely gone — and even if present, analyte stability would need checking.

options.text: Yes — urine is kept for 7 days
options.rationale: Incorrect. Seven days is the recommendation for blood and body-fluid smears, not urine.

options.text: Yes — all clinical pathology specimens are kept for 2 years
options.rationale: Incorrect. Two years is the retention for records such as patient test records, not for the specimens themselves.

options.text: Yes — urine is kept for 48 hours like serum
options.rationale: Incorrect. Serum, plasma, CSF and other body fluids are kept 48 hours, but urine is the exception at 24 hours.

questions.skill: Apply specimen retention to add-on requests

questions.stem: An accredited lab keeps surgical pathology paraffin blocks for 10 years. An inspector asks what the federal CLIA minimum is. Which answer is correct?

options.text: 2 years — the 10-year period is a CAP recommendation that exceeds CLIA
options.rationale: Correct. CLIA requires pathology specimen blocks to be kept at least 2 years; CAP recommends 10 years, which meets or exceeds the federal minimum.

options.text: 10 years — CLIA and CAP are identical
options.rationale: Incorrect. For blocks they differ: CLIA 2 years, CAP 10 years. (CLIA does require 10 years for histopathology slides and pathology reports.)
Incorrect. Five years is the CLIA period for cytology slides, not paraffin blocks.
Incorrect. "Until diagnosis" is the CLIA rule for remnants of tissue, not for blocks.
